item.title: Linux: The Foundation of Modern DevOps
item.description:
Linux: The Foundation of Modern DevOps

Linux powers nearly everything on the Internet.

Whether you browse a website, stream a movie, deploy an application, or use cloud services, chances are Linux is running somewhere in the background.

If you want to become a DevOps Engineer, Cloud Engineer, Site Reliability Engineer (SRE), Platform Engineer, or Backend Developer, Linux is the first skill you should master.

This guide explains Linux from the ground up with practical examples and projects.

item.title: Building a Production-Grade PDF-to-Markdown OCR Pipeline on Manjaro Linux: Lessons in Arch, PEP 668, and PyCharm
item.description:
Converting scanned PDFs into structured formats like Markdown (.md) and Rich Text Format (.rtf) while preserving table structures, removing page headers/footers, and maintaining heading hierarchies is one of the most common document processing challenges.

However, implementing this on an Arch-based Linux distribution like Manjaro presents unique challenges due to Python’s system protections (PEP 668), shell behavior across external drive mounts, and shifting package interfaces.

This blog provides a complete step-by-step guide to building a robust document conversion pipeline using Python, marker-pdf, pandoc, and PyCharm on Manjaro Linux.

item.title: Building an Autonomous Mobile & Desktop Document Processing AI Agent with OpenClaw
item.description:
Setting up a self-hosted AI agent that does more than just chat opens up incredible automation possibilities. By combining an open-source agentic framework with lightweight system utilities, you can turn a low-power phone or a modest desktop into a 24/7 personal document processing hub.

This guide walks through configuring OpenClaw (formerly known as Clawdbot) across Android Termux and Linux Mint, setting up messaging channel integrations, running local LLMs, and defining custom Markdown skills to automatically clean, compress, and OCR scanned office documents.

item.title: Bypassing CMOS Clock Failure on Linux with Automated Network Time Sync
item.description:
Overview

A depleted or faulty CMOS battery causes system clocks to reset to an epoch date (e.g., January 1, 1970) upon every power cycle. On modern Linux distributions, an incorrect system time breaks SSL/TLS certificate validation, systemd timers, package manager operations, and secure web browsing.

While replacing the motherboard RTC battery is the ideal physical fix, system-level automation provides an immediate software workaround by forcing network time synchronization immediately after the network interface comes online.

item.title: Bypassing Faulty CMOS Batteries in Linux Mint and Manjaro with Automated Network Time Sync
item.description:
Dealing with a faulty or dead motherboard CMOS battery can be a frustrating experience on Linux systems. Every cold boot resets the system clock—often back to 2010 or 1970—causing broken SSL/TLS certificates, failing web browsers, broken package manager updates, and out-of-sync system logs.

While replacing the CR2032 battery is the hardware fix, you can completely automate the recovery process in software so your computer seamlessly adjusts to the correct local time within seconds of booting up.

item.title: Dual-Booting Done Right: How to Seamlessly Share Storage Between Linux and Windows
item.description:
Dual-Booting Done Right: How to Seamlessly Share Storage Between Linux and Windows

The temptation to pick up your entire /home directory and drop it straight onto an NTFS drive is strong. It seems like the cleanest, fastest fix. But if you have ever tried it, you probably met a wall of login loops, broken desktop themes, or weird permission errors.

item.description:

item.title: The Ultimate Guide to Customizing the Linux Mint Boot Experience: Plymouth Themes, Custom Logos, and Silent Boot
item.description:
The Ultimate Guide to Customizing the Linux Mint Boot Experience

There is something deeply satisfying about tailoring an operating system to feel uniquely yours. While tweaking desktop wallpapers, icon packs, panel layouts, and GTK themes is standard practice for Linux Mint users, the boot screen is often left completely untouched.

When you turn on your PC, you are greeted by the standard Linux Mint logo pulsating against a dark background. This boot splash screen—managed by an underlying framework called Plymouth—is fully customizable. Whether you want to swap the standard Mint logo for your own personal logo or wallpaper, install an animated high-tech theme, fix stretched low-resolution boot graphics, or disable graphics entirely to view real-time system logs during startup, this guide covers every step in detail.

item.title: The Ultimate Guide to Managing Swap Space and Swappiness in Linux Mint
item.description:
The Ultimate Guide to Managing Swap Space and Swappiness in Linux Mint

If your system runs low on physical RAM, Linux utilizes Swap memory as a safety net. Swap acts as a extension of your system’s RAM by allocating space on your storage drive (SSD or HDD). When physical memory is saturated, the kernel offloads inactive memory pages into swap, keeping your desktop responsive and preventing application crashes caused by Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors.

item.title: Troubleshooting Linux Boot Failures and Optimizing Linux Mint Performance
item.description:
Dealing with boot errors can be daunting, but Linux gives you full control to inspect, repair, and optimize your system. In this comprehensive guide, we cover how to fix missing EFI bootloaders, format and rebuild GRUB from scratch using live environment tools, and squeeze maximum performance out of Linux Mint.

Part 1: Resolving the “failed to open /efi/ubuntu not found” Error

When your system fails to boot and displays the error failed to open /efi/ubuntu not found, it means the UEFI firmware or GRUB bootloader cannot locate the necessary EFI binaries to start the OS. This typically occurs after major Windows updates in dual-boot setups, disk partition changes, or corrupted EFI filesystems.

item.title: Troubleshooting Linux Mint Wi-Fi Drops: From Hardware Drivers to Automated NTP Time Sync
item.description:
Troubleshooting Linux Mint Wi-Fi Drops: From Hardware Drivers to Automated NTP Time Sync

Experiencing random Wi-Fi disconnections on Linux Mint—where the network suddenly drops and all available Wi-Fi access points disappear from the menu—is a surprisingly common frustration.

While this issue is often caused by aggressive driver power management or missing proprietary modules, another common underlying culprit is system clock drift. When your local system clock drifts out of alignment with remote authentication servers, security handshakes silently fail, dropping your wireless connection.
